high-rise-leggings-woman.short: High-rise training leggings built for squatting, lifting and conditioning, with a waistband that stays put. Women's S to XL.
body: A high-rise cut that sits above the hip and stays there through squats, hinges and floor work, so the last set is not spent pulling a waistband back into place.
Cut for training rather than for the walk in: the rise holds under load, the fabric moves with the joint, and the pair survives the wash cycle a gym wardrobe actually puts it through.
features: High-rise waistband that holds through squats and hinges
Cut to move through a full range of motion

long-sleeve-tee-unisex.short: A unisex long-sleeve training tee for cooler sessions and early starts, cut to move rather than to cling. Sizes S to XL.
body: A long-sleeve tee for the sessions that start cold and do not stay that way — enough cover for a winter warm-up, light enough to keep working once the room heats up.
Unisex sizing from S to XL, cut straight through the body so it layers over a tank without bunching under a rig or a bar.
features: Long sleeve for cooler sessions and early starts

oversized-hoodie-unisex.short: The unisex oversized MasterKraft hoodie: a relaxed-fit layer for warm-ups, cool-downs and rest days. Sizes S to XL.
body: Cut oversized on purpose. It goes on over a tee without dragging, sits loose through the shoulder, and does the job a gym hoodie is actually bought for — keeping warmth in between working sets and on the way home.
Unisex sizing from S to XL.
features: Relaxed oversized cut through body and shoulder
Layers over training kit without pulling

oversized-tee-unisex.short: A unisex oversized training tee with room through the body and shoulder, for lifting without a sleeve in the way. Sizes S to XL.
body: Cut with room through the body and shoulder so nothing binds at the top of a press or the bottom of a squat — an oversized tee that is oversized where it helps.
Unisex sizing from S to XL.
features: Room through body and shoulder for overhead work

relaxed-short-sleeve-tee-woman.short: A relaxed-fit women's training tee that moves with the session instead of clinging to it. Sizes S to XL.
body: A relaxed cut through the body, so it skims rather than clings — the tee for a session where the plan is to stop thinking about what you are wearing.
Women's sizing from S to XL.

short-sleeve-polo-male.short: A men's short-sleeve polo for coaches and floor staff who need to look the part and still demonstrate a lift. Sizes S to XL.
body: The collar that works on a gym floor: smart enough for a member consultation, cut loose enough to demonstrate a clean without the shoulder seam objecting.
Men's sizing from S to XL. A sensible default for coaching staff and front-of-house uniform.
features: Cut to allow a full demonstration range

short-sleeve-tee-male.short: The everyday men's MasterKraft training tee — straightforward, cut to move, and built for the wash cycle a gym wardrobe demands. Sizes S to XL.
body: The plain one. A short-sleeve training tee with no feature list to memorise: it fits, it moves, and it goes back in the bag for tomorrow.
Men's sizing from S to XL.

socks.short: MasterKraft training socks — the cushioning and grip that lifting flat and running intervals both ask for.
body: The piece of kit nobody photographs and everybody notices when it is wrong. Enough cushioning for intervals, enough hold to stop a sock migrating into an arch mid-set.
Unisex.

sports-bra-woman.short: A women's training sports bra built for lifting and conditioning, with support that holds through the work. Sizes S to XL.
body: Support that holds through the parts of a session that test it — jumps, sprints, and the moment a bar is racked. Cut to stay where it was put.
Women's sizing from S to XL.
features: Support through jumping and conditioning work
Cut to stay in place under load

sweat-towel.short: A MasterKraft sweat towel for the bench, the bar and the rower — gym-sized, and built for a commercial wash.
body: Sized for a bench and a pair of hands rather than a bathroom rail, and built to survive being washed as often as a gym washes towels.
The one piece of equipment every member is asked to bring and half of them forget — worth stocking at the front desk.

sweatshirt-unisex.short: A unisex crew-neck training sweatshirt for warm-ups, cool-downs and cold starts. Sizes S to XL.
body: A crew-neck sweatshirt without a hood getting in the way of a bar — the layer for a cold warm-up that comes off by the second set.
Unisex sizing from S to XL.
features: Crew neck, nothing to catch under a bar

tank-male.short: A men's training tank cut for heat, overhead work and the sessions where sleeves are the enemy. Sizes S to XL.
body: Open through the shoulder, which is the point: pressing overhead, pulling, and anything in a room that has given up on air conditioning.
Men's sizing from S to XL.
features: Open through the shoulder for overhead work

tank-woman.short: A women's training tank cut for heat and overhead work, with room to move through the shoulder. Sizes S to XL.
body: Cut open through the shoulder for pressing and pulling, and light enough for the sessions where the room is doing half the conditioning work.
Women's sizing from S to XL.

train-cap.short: The MasterKraft Train cap — for outdoor conditioning, sled work and keeping sweat and sun out of the session.
body: For the sessions that happen outside: sled pushes on turf, carries in a car park, conditioning in full sun.
Unisex, one size.

training-shorts-7-male.short: Men's 7-inch training shorts, cut short enough to squat and lunge without the hem deciding otherwise. Sizes S to XL.
body: A 7-inch inseam, which is the length that stops a hem catching at the bottom of a squat or riding up through a lunge — short enough to move, long enough to wear on a gym floor.
Men's sizing from S to XL.
features: 7-inch inseam, cut for squatting and lunging

agility-dots-set-of-5.short: A set of five low-profile agility dots for footwork drills, reaction work and marking out a conditioning circuit.
body: Five flat markers for footwork patterns, reaction drills and change-of-direction work — low enough to run over without turning an ankle, visible enough to coach from across the floor.
The cheapest way to turn an empty square of floor into a drill, and light enough that a coach can carry the whole set in one hand between stations.
features: Low profile, safe to run over

eva-exercise-mat-set-of-10.short: Ten EVA foam exercise mats — the floor-work set for a studio, a stretching zone or a group fitness room.
body: A set of ten EVA foam mats, bought the way a gym actually needs them: enough for a class, a stretching corner or a full studio floor rather than one at a time.
EVA is the sensible choice for shared matting — it wipes down, it holds its shape under repeated rolling, and it does not absorb what a busy floor puts on it.
features: Set of ten, sized for a class or studio floor
EVA foam — wipes down and holds its shape
Floor work, stretching and group fitness

fitness-ball.short: Anti-burst fitness balls in 55cm, 65cm and 75cm, for core work, mobility, stability and rehab programming.
body: Three diameters, because the right ball is the one that matches the athlete: 55cm, 65cm and 75cm, all anti-burst.
Anti-burst is the specification that matters in a commercial room. A ball that deflates slowly rather than failing outright is the difference between an interrupted set and an incident report.
features: Core, mobility, stability and rehab work

foam-plyometric-box.short: Foam plyometric boxes in 6, 12 and 24 inch heights — jump training without the shin the timber version costs.
body: Foam plyo boxes in 6, 12 and 24 inch heights, for jump training, step-ups and progressions that need a forgiving landing surface.

The argument for foam over timber is the miss. A missed box jump on a plywood edge ends a training block; the same miss on foam ends a rep. For group classes and mixed-ability floors that trade is worth making.
features: Foam construction — forgiving on a missed jump
Jump training, step-ups and plyometric progressions

massage-rolling-machine.short: A massage rolling machine for recovery zones — assisted soft-tissue work without a member having to get on the floor.
body: Soft-tissue work that does not require a member to get down onto a mat and back up again, which is what keeps recovery in a programme rather than in theory.
A sensible anchor for a recovery corner, alongside rollers and mats.

micro-bands.short: Micro bands in Heavy, X Heavy and XX Heavy — glute activation, warm-ups and banded accessory work.
body: Short-loop bands for activation and accessory work: banded walks, glute work, warm-up sets and the small-range work that makes the big lifts move.
Three resistances — Heavy, X Heavy and XX Heavy — so a warm-up can progress rather than staying where it started.
features: Heavy, X Heavy and XX Heavy
Short loop, for activation and accessory work
Warm-ups, glute work and banded walks

power-bands.short: Power bands in 13mm red, 21mm grey and 32mm black — assisted pull-ups, accommodating resistance and mobility work.
body: Long-loop resistance bands in three widths: 13mm red, 21mm grey and 32mm black. Assisted pull-ups, banded squats and presses, mobility work and stretching.
Colour-coded by width so a coach can call a band from across the floor and get the right one back.
features: Assisted pull-ups, accommodating resistance and mobility

station-markers-set-of-20.short: A set of twenty station markers for laying out circuits, class stations and conditioning courses.
body: Twenty markers, which is enough to lay out a full circuit, number a class, or set the course for a conditioning session and still have spares.
The bulk set exists because a gym never needs one marker. It needs the floor mapped before a class walks in.
features: Circuit layout, class stations and conditioning courses

concept-2-bike-erg-with-pm5-monitor.short: The Concept2 BikeErg with PM5 monitor, supplied by MasterKraft — air resistance and the PM5's measured, repeatable data.
body: The Concept2 BikeErg with the PM5 performance monitor. Air resistance scales with effort, so the machine gives back exactly what is put in, and the PM5 records it in numbers that mean the same thing on every machine in the room.
That repeatability is why BikeErgs end up in testing protocols and class programming: a result from one machine can be compared to a result from another, and to the same athlete three months ago.
features: Air resistance — output scales with effort

concept-2-row-erg-with-standard-legs.short: The Concept2 RowErg with standard legs, supplied by MasterKraft — the rower commercial testing and class programming is written around.
body: The Concept2 RowErg on standard legs, in the configuration most commercial floors buy. Air resistance, and the PM5's measured output.
It is the default for a reason: the numbers are comparable between machines and between gyms, which makes it the machine that testing protocols and class programming are written around.
features: Air resistance with measured, comparable output

concept-2-ski-erg-floor-stand.short: The Concept2 floor stand for the SkiErg — freestanding installation where a wall mount is not an option.
body: The floor stand that makes a SkiErg freestanding, for floors where a wall mount is not available or not wanted — glass, a partition, or a layout that needs to move.
Ordered alongside a SkiErg, or after one, when a room gets rearranged.

concept-2-ski-erg-with-pm5.short: The Concept2 SkiErg with PM5 monitor, supplied by MasterKraft — upper-body and full-body conditioning with measured output.
body: The Concept2 SkiErg with the PM5 performance monitor. Double-poling drives the full posterior chain through the trunk and arms, which makes it the conditioning piece that reaches what rowers and bikes do not.
The PM5 gives it the same comparable, repeatable output as the rest of the Concept2 range, so it programmes the same way.
features: Comparable output across the Concept2 range

performance-indoor-cycle.short: A commercial indoor cycle for studio classes and conditioning floors, built for back-to-back sessions.
body: An indoor cycle specified for a commercial room rather than a spare bedroom: built for consecutive classes, repeated adjustment by different riders, and the cleaning schedule a studio floor runs on.
Suited to group cycling programming and to conditioning floors where a bike has to survive being used all day.

performance-reformer.short: A Pilates reformer specified for commercial studios — the performance model, built for a full class timetable.
body: A reformer for a studio running a full timetable: carriage, springs and footbar built to take continuous class use rather than occasional home sessions.

MasterKraft supplies reformers as part of studio fit-outs, so a floor of them arrives matched and at the same time. See our fit-out service if you are building a studio rather than replacing a machine.
features: Available as part of a matched studio fit-out

studio-reformer.short: A studio Pilates reformer built for continuous class use, available matched across a full studio floor.
body: The studio reformer: built for the repetition a class timetable puts through a carriage and a spring set, and specified so a room of them stays consistent.
Reformers are commonly bought a floor at a time rather than one at a time. We supply and install them as a matched set — see our fit-out service.
features: Supplied matched across a studio floor

3rd-tier-for-ifdb4.short: A third tier for the IFDB4 dumbbell rack, available as clearance stock — added storage height without a second rack.
body: The third-tier add-on for the IFDB4 dumbbell rack: more storage in the same footprint, which is the only direction a full dumbbell floor can grow.
Clearance stock — ex-display, limited to what is on hand. Contact us to confirm availability before planning a floor around it.

functional-trainer-clearance.short: A functional trainer available as clearance stock — dual-cable training in a single footprint, at ex-display pricing.
body: A dual-cable functional trainer: adjustable pulleys covering presses, pulls, rotations and the cable accessory work a floor needs, in one footprint.
Clearance stock — ex-display and limited to what is on hand, so pricing is sharper than new and quantity is not repeatable. Contact us to confirm what is available.

hoist-drv10.short: A Hoist DRV10 available as clearance stock — commercial-grade selectorised strength at ex-display pricing.
body: A Hoist DRV10, offered as clearance. Hoist build selectorised machines for commercial floors, and a piece coming off display is the cheapest way onto that standard.
Ex-display stock, limited to what is on hand. Contact us to confirm condition and availability.

leg-attachment-for-home-gym.short: A leg attachment for a home gym cable station, available as clearance stock — leg curl and extension without a second machine.
body: The attachment that adds leg curl and leg extension to a home gym cable station, so the lower body is not left to bodyweight alone.
Clearance stock — ex-display and limited. Check compatibility with your station with us before ordering.

olympic-power-bar-20kg-2200mm-700lb-capa.short: A 20kg Olympic power bar, 2200mm, rated to 700lb, available as clearance stock.
body: A 20kg Olympic bar at 2200mm with a 700lb capacity rating — a full-length power bar for squatting, pressing and pulling.
Clearance stock, limited to what is on hand. The specification above is the bar's own; contact us to confirm condition.

olympic-weight-plate-tree-csl10n.short: An Olympic weight plate tree (CSL10N) available as clearance stock — plate storage that keeps a platform clear.
body: A vertical plate tree for Olympic plates: gets the plates off the floor and into one place, which is most of what keeps a platform safe to walk around.
Clearance stock — ex-display, limited to what is on hand.

barbell-storage-box.short: A freestanding barbell storage box — vertical bar storage that keeps bars off the floor and out of the walkway.
body: Vertical storage for barbells, freestanding so it can sit where the bars are used rather than where a wall happens to be.
Bars left on the floor are the most common trip hazard on a lifting floor and the fastest way to damage a knurl. A box fixes both, and it takes a fraction of the floor a rack of horizontal bars does.
features: Keeps bars off the floor and out of walkways

modular-storage-rack-complete.short: The complete modular storage rack — the full configuration, for consolidating a floor's accessories into one unit.
body: The modular storage rack in its complete configuration, supplied as a whole rather than built up shelf by shelf.
Modular storage earns its place on a busy floor by putting dumbbells, balls, bands and mats in one addressed location, so the floor resets between classes instead of drifting.
features: Complete configuration, supplied as one unit
Consolidates accessory storage into one footprint

wall-mounted-battle-rope-storage.short: Wall-mounted battle rope storage — gets ropes off the floor, coiled and ready for the next session.
body: A wall mount for battle ropes. Coiled and hung, a rope stays untangled and out of the walkway; left on the floor it is both a trip hazard and a five-minute job to sort out before the next class.
Wall-mounted, so it costs no floor space at all.

wall-mounted-exercise-mat-hanging-rack.short: A wall-mounted hanging rack for exercise mats — mats stored upright, drying and out of the way.
body: Mats hung rather than stacked, which is the difference between a mat that dries and one that does not. Upright storage also makes it obvious when mats have gone missing.
Wall-mounted, so a studio or stretching zone loses no floor to storage.

wall-mounted-rope-and-band-rack.short: A wall-mounted rope and band rack — one addressed home for the accessories that otherwise end up everywhere.
body: Bands and ropes are the accessories most likely to end up draped over a rig, and the ones members most often cannot find. A wall rack gives them one place to be returned to.
Wall-mounted, so it adds storage without taking floor.
features: One addressed home for ropes and bands

wall-mounted-rope-and-band-rack-small.short: The small wall-mounted rope and band rack — the same storage for a narrower wall or a smaller accessory set.
body: The compact version of the rope and band rack, for a narrower run of wall or a smaller accessory set — a studio, a PT room, or a corner of a larger floor.
Wall-mounted, so it costs no floor space.
features: Suits studios, PT rooms and smaller accessory sets

acoustic-underlay-1m-x-10m.short: Acoustic underlay in 1m x 10m rolls, at 5mm, 10mm, 15mm and 20mm — impact and noise control under a gym floor.
body: Acoustic underlay in 1m x 10m rolls, in four thicknesses: 5mm, 10mm, 15mm and 20mm. It goes under the finished floor to control impact noise and vibration.

Thickness is a decision about what is below you. A ground-floor slab and a first-floor tenancy above an office are different problems, and the second one is usually the reason a gym gets a noise complaint. Talk to us about the build-up before ordering.
features: Impact and vibration control under the finished floor

artificial-turf-black-2m-x-15m.short: Black artificial turf, 2m x 15m — a sled track and functional training surface in a 15 metre run.
body: A 2m x 15m run of black artificial turf: the surface for sled pushes and pulls, prowler work and functional training lanes.
Fifteen metres is the common indoor track length — long enough to programme a real push, short enough for most floors to fit.
features: Sled tracks and functional training lanes

artificial-turf-black-2m-x-20m.short: Black artificial turf, 2m x 20m — the longer sled track run, for floors with room to programme distance.
body: A 2m x 20m run of black artificial turf, for floors that can take a longer track. Five extra metres changes what can be programmed on it: longer pushes, sprint work, and distance intervals that do not turn around.
The same surface as the 15m run, in a longer roll.

artificial-turf-green-2m-x-15m.short: Green artificial turf, 2m x 15m — a sled and functional training lane where the floor should read as grass.
body: A 2m x 15m run of green artificial turf. Same job as the black — sleds, prowlers, functional lanes — with a surface that reads as grass rather than as gym floor.
The choice is usually about the room: green suits studios and outdoor-styled zones where black reads heavy.
features: Sled tracks and functional training lanes

commercial-rubber-tiles.short: Commercial rubber floor tiles — the working surface for free-weight floors, laid tile by tile and replaced the same way.
body: Rubber tiles for commercial free-weight floors: the surface that takes dropped plates, protects the slab, and keeps noise down.
Tiles rather than rolls is a maintenance decision. When one section takes a beating under a platform or a dumbbell rack, a tile floor is repaired by replacing that tile instead of relaying a room.
features: Tile format — damaged sections replaced individually
Free-weight floors, dumbbell zones and platforms

led-dimmer.short: An LED dimmer for the Linear LED Lighting System — class lighting that changes with the session.
body: The dimmer control for the Linear LED Lighting System. Lighting that comes down for a cool-down and up for a working set is standard in boutique studios, and it is a control problem before it is a lighting one.
Specified alongside the linear system as part of a fit-out.

linear-led-lighting-system.short: A linear LED lighting system for gym and studio fit-outs — the overhead run that finishes a room.
body: Linear LED lighting for gym and studio ceilings: continuous runs that light a floor evenly rather than dropping pools of light between fittings, which is what makes a rig line look deliberate.
Supplied as part of MasterKraft fit-outs, with the matching dimmer where a room needs class lighting that changes through a session.
features: Continuous linear runs for even floor lighting
Pairs with the LED Dimmer for class lighting
Specified as part of a gym or studio fit-out

aerobic-weighted-exercise-bars.short: Aerobic weighted exercise bars in 4kg, 6kg and 8kg — the group fitness bar for pump-style classes.
body: Weighted bars in 4kg, 6kg and 8kg for group fitness: squats, presses, rows and lunges at a load a full class can hold for a whole track.
Three weights is what lets one class serve a mixed room — the same programme, three entry points, no one sitting out.
features: Group fitness and pump-style class programming

aerobic-weighted-exercise-bars-10kg.short: The 10kg aerobic weighted exercise bar — the top of the group fitness bar range, for stronger class members.
body: The 10kg bar: the step up from the 4-6-8kg run, for class members who have outgrown it and would otherwise be under-loaded for a whole track.
Bought individually rather than as a set, because a room usually needs a handful of these rather than a full rack.

aqua-bag.short: An aqua bag — water-filled instability training for carries, cleans and the core work a static load cannot reach.
body: A water-filled training bag. The load shifts as it moves, so the body has to stabilise continuously rather than just resist a fixed weight — which is the whole point of it.
Carries, cleans, squats and overhead work all change character with water in the bag. It also fills and empties, so the same bag covers several loads and stores flat.
features: Water-filled — the load shifts through the movement
Fills and empties to vary load
Carries, cleans, squats and overhead work

chrome-dumbbell-set-1kg-10kg-pairs.short: A chrome dumbbell set in 1kg to 10kg pairs — the light end of a studio or PT floor, in one purchase.
body: Chrome dumbbells in pairs from 1kg to 10kg: the light end of the range, which is the half a studio, PT room or rehab space uses most.
Bought as a set rather than a pair at a time, so the increments are complete on day one and a programme never stalls on a missing weight.

chrome-110-dumbbells-1kg-7kg-pairs.short: Chrome 110 dumbbells in 1kg to 7kg pairs — a compact light-weight set for studios and rehab work.
body: The Chrome 110 range in pairs from 1kg to 7kg — a shorter run than the full set, for rooms where the heavy end is never used.
Suits studios, group fitness rooms and rehab spaces where the demand sits at the light end and floor space does not allow for weights nobody picks up.
features: Compact range for studios and rehab

climbing-rope.short: A climbing rope for rigs and functional zones — vertical pulling that no machine substitutes for.
body: A climbing rope for a rig or a ceiling anchor. Rope climbs load the grip, the arms and the trunk together in a way no machine reproduces, which is why they stay in functional programming.
Fixing matters as much as the rope: talk to us about anchor points if this is going into an existing rig rather than a planned fit-out.
features: Grip, upper body and trunk under one movement
Mounts to a rig or ceiling anchor

cotton-inners.short: Cotton inner wraps for boxing — the layer between hand and glove that keeps a shared glove wearable.
body: Cotton inners worn under a boxing glove: they support the hand and take the sweat that would otherwise go straight into the glove.
For a gym running boxing classes with shared gloves, inners are what makes that arrangement acceptable to members. Stocked at the desk, they are a small sale that solves a real problem.

group-fitness-barbell-set-collars-pr.short: A group fitness barbell set with collars, supplied per pair — the class bar and its locking collars together.
body: The group fitness barbell set supplied with its collars, per pair, so a class bar arrives complete rather than needing collars sourced separately.
Collars are the part that goes missing first in a group fitness room, and a bar without them is a bar nobody should load.

group-fitness-step-4-risers.short: A group fitness step with four risers — adjustable step height for mixed-ability class programming.
body: A class step supplied with four risers, so height adjusts to the member rather than the member adjusting to the step.
Four risers covers the range a mixed class needs: a low platform for beginners and a full height for the people who have been there a while, without buying two products.

olympic-dumbbell-handles-pair.short: A pair of Olympic dumbbell handles — loadable dumbbells built from the plates a floor already has.
body: Olympic-spec dumbbell handles, sold in pairs. Loaded with the plates already on the floor, they cover the whole dumbbell range without buying the whole dumbbell range.

The economic argument is straightforward: a loadable pair plus existing plates replaces a rack of fixed dumbbells, at a fraction of the floor space and the spend. The trade is the time spent changing plates between sets.
features: Olympic sleeve — takes standard Olympic plates
Full dumbbell range from plates already on the floor

pilates-ring.short: A Pilates ring for studio and mat work — resistance for inner thigh, arm and core sequences.
body: The magic circle: a sprung ring that adds resistance to inner thigh, arm and core work in mat and reformer sequences.
Light, cheap and stackable, which is why studios buy them by the set rather than individually.
features: Resistance for inner thigh, arm and core work

urethane-fixed-dumbbells-pair.short: Urethane fixed dumbbells, sold per pair — the commercial-floor dumbbell, bought one increment at a time.
body: Urethane fixed dumbbells by the pair, for filling a gap in an existing rack or building a range up one increment at a time.
Urethane is the finish commercial floors settle on: it takes being dropped, it does not mark the floor the way cast iron does, and it keeps its colour and its printed weight far longer than rubber.
features: Fills gaps in an existing dumbbell range

wall-ball-armatex.short: Armatex wall balls in 4kg, 6kg, 8kg, 9kg and 10kg — the class-floor wall ball, in five loads.
body: Wall balls in Armatex, from 4kg to 10kg across five loads: 4, 6, 8, 9 and 10kg. Wall ball shots, cleans, throws and carries.
Armatex is the shell that survives a class floor. A wall ball is thrown at a wall hundreds of times a day, and the seam is what fails first — which is the whole argument for the covering.
features: Wall ball shots, cleans and throws

wall-ball-armatex-12kg.short: The 12kg Armatex wall ball — the heavy end, above the standard 4kg to 10kg run.
body: The 12kg wall ball: above the standard range, for stronger athletes and for programming that wants a genuine top end.
Same Armatex shell as the rest of the range, bought individually because a floor needs a few rather than a rack.

dead-balls-set-of-4.short: A set of four dead balls — non-bouncing slam and throw work, bought as a floor's worth rather than one at a time.
body: Four dead balls as a set. A dead ball does not bounce, which is what makes it safe to slam and throw at full effort indoors.
Sold as a set of four because that is how a conditioning station is staffed — enough for a small group to work simultaneously rather than queue.

power-bags-set-of-6.short: A set of six power bags — the full conditioning station, for carries, cleans, squats and throws.
body: Six power bags as a set: enough to run a station for a group rather than rotating one bag through a queue.
Power bags cover carries, cleans, squats, lunges and throws with one implement, which is why they earn their floor space in a room programming circuits.
features: Set of six — a full station
Carries, cleans, squats, lunges and throws

rubber-hex-dumbbell-set-of-14-pairs.short: A rubber hex dumbbell set of 14 pairs — a complete dumbbell range for a commercial floor in one purchase.
body: Fourteen pairs of rubber hex dumbbells, bought as a complete range. The hex shape stops them rolling and lets them sit flat for renegade rows and push-ups.
A set is how a floor should be bought: the increments are complete from the first day, and no programme stalls because one weight was never ordered.
features: Rubber hex — will not roll, sits flat

urethane-competition-kettlebell-set-of-5.short: A set of five urethane competition kettlebells — uniform-dimension bells for consistent technique across loads.
body: Five urethane competition kettlebells. Competition bells share the same dimensions regardless of weight, so the handle and the bell sit the same way against the forearm at every load.
That consistency is the reason to buy competition over cast: technique transfers directly as the weight goes up, instead of having to be relearned on a bigger bell.

urethane-fixed-dumbbells-set-1-10kg-pair.short: Urethane fixed dumbbells in 1kg to 10kg pairs, supplied with a vertical dumbbell rack — a complete light-end station.
body: The light end of the urethane range in pairs from 1kg to 10kg, supplied with the vertical rack to hold it. A complete station rather than a set of dumbbells and a storage problem.
Vertical racking is the right call for a light range: it holds the full run in a footprint a horizontal rack would use for half of it.
features: Supplied with a vertical dumbbell rack

wall-ball-armatex-set-of-4.short: A set of four Armatex wall balls — a full wall ball station for class and small-group programming.
body: Four Armatex wall balls as a set, which is a station rather than an implement: enough for a small group to work at once.
Same Armatex shell as the individual balls, bought the way a class floor actually needs them.
features: Set of four — a full station

2-cell-rack-with-storage.short: A two-cell rack with integrated storage — two lifting stations and their plate storage in one structure.
body: Two working cells with storage built into the frame, so the plates live where they are used instead of on a tree across the room.
Two cells is the unit most small floors start from: enough for two lifters or a coach and an athlete, and it extends into a longer rig later rather than being replaced.
features: Extends into a longer rig line

functional-training-system-1-0.short: Functional Training System 1.0 — the entry configuration, for PT studios and compact functional zones.
body: The smallest configuration in the Functional Training System range: a single functional training footprint for a PT studio, a small group room, or a corner of a larger floor.
The range is built to scale, so a 1.0 is a starting point rather than a ceiling — the configurations above it extend the same system. Talk to us about which size suits your floor plan.
features: PT studios and compact functional zones

functional-training-system-2-0.short: Functional Training System 2.0 — the second configuration, sized for small-group training rather than one-to-one.
body: A step up from the 1.0: sized for small-group training, where two or three people work at once rather than a coach and a single athlete.

That is usually the point a PT studio outgrows its first system — the programming stops being one-to-one and the floor has to keep up. Talk to us about the configuration that matches your class sizes.

functional-training-system-3-0.short: Functional Training System 3.0 — the mid configuration, for a functional zone inside a full commercial floor.
body: The middle of the range, and the size most often specified as the functional zone within a larger commercial gym — substantial enough to anchor a room without taking the whole floor.
Sits naturally alongside a free-weight area and a cardio line. Talk to us about how it lands in your layout.
features: Anchors a functional zone in a commercial floor
Works alongside free-weight and cardio areas

functional-training-system-4-0.short: Functional Training System 4.0 — a large configuration, for floors running functional classes at volume.
body: A large configuration, for rooms where functional training is a timetabled class rather than a corner of the gym — enough stations to run a group through without queueing.
At this size the decision is as much about floor plan and traffic flow as it is about the system. We plan these as part of a fit-out.
features: Planned as part of a floor layout

functional-training-system-5-0.short: Functional Training System 5.0 — the largest configuration, for full functional floors and performance facilities.
body: The top of the range: the configuration specified for a full functional floor or a performance facility, where the system is the room rather than a zone in it.
A 5.0 is a fit-out decision, not a purchase decision — layout, ceiling height, flooring and traffic flow all come into it. Talk to us before it goes into a plan.
features: Full functional floors and performance facilities

olympic-half-rack-wall-mounted.short: A wall-mounted Olympic half rack — full squat and press capability with the floor left clear.
body: The half rack fixed to the wall rather than standing on the floor. Same squatting and pressing capability, no base footprint, and a clear floor around it.

Wall mounting is what makes a half rack viable in a narrow room or a space that has to convert between uses. It does require a wall that will take the load — talk to us about fixings before it is specified.

olympic-half-rack-2-0.short: The Olympic Half Rack 2.0 — the updated freestanding half rack for commercial squat and press work.
body: The second-generation half rack: freestanding, for squatting, pressing and rack pulls without the full footprint of a power rack.
A half rack is the right answer for most commercial floors. It gives a lifter the working height and the safety of a rack while taking roughly half the floor a four-post cage does.
features: Squat, press and rack pull work
Half the footprint of a full power rack

olympic-half-rack-with-dead-lift.short: An Olympic half rack with an integrated deadlift platform — rack work and pulling in one footprint.
body: The half rack with a deadlift station built in, so squatting, pressing and pulling all happen in one place instead of across two.

For a floor short on space this is the combination that matters most: the deadlift is the lift most often displaced to a corner, and integrating it keeps the platform where the bar and the plates already are.
features: Squat, press and pull in one footprint

olympic-half-rack-with-dual-pulley.short: An Olympic half rack with dual pulleys — free-weight rack work and full cable training in one station.
body: A half rack with dual pulleys built into the uprights: squatting and pressing on the rack, and the whole cable vocabulary — pulls, presses, rotations, accessory work — from the same station.
One footprint doing two jobs, which is the most efficient square metre on a mixed commercial floor.
features: Free-weight rack work and cable training combined

olympic-half-rack-with-dual-pulley-wall-.short: A wall-mounted Olympic half rack with dual pulleys — rack and cable training with no floor footprint.
body: The dual-pulley half rack fixed to the wall: rack work and full cable training, with the floor in front of it left completely clear.

The configuration for a room that has to do everything and has no space to do it in — a boutique studio, a hotel gym, or a floor that converts between classes and open use. Wall fixing needs to be checked; talk to us before specifying.
features: Rack and cable work in a single fixed station

olympic-power-rack-5-0.short: The Olympic Power Rack 5.0 — a full four-post cage for heavy squatting, pressing and pulling.
body: A full power rack: four posts, enclosed working area, and the safety to let a lifter fail a heavy squat on their own.
That is the case for a cage over a half rack. It takes more floor, and in exchange a lifter can work to genuine limits without a spotter — which is what an unstaffed or 24-hour floor needs.
features: Enclosed working area for unspotted lifting
Heavy squat, press and pull work

olympic-power-rack-with-dual-pulley.short: An Olympic power rack with dual pulleys — a full cage and a complete cable station in one structure.
body: The full four-post cage with dual pulleys integrated: heavy barbell work inside the rack, cable work from the same frame.
The most complete single station on a commercial floor. For a room buying one piece of equipment to cover the widest programme, this is usually it.
features: Four-post cage with integrated dual pulleys
Barbell and cable training in one structure
The most complete single station on a floor

smith-machine.short: A Smith machine — guided barbell work for solo lifters, rehab progressions and high-volume accessory training.
body: A barbell on a fixed path. The bar cannot travel out of plane, so a lifter can push close to failure without a spotter and can be loaded safely through a rehab progression.
On a commercial floor it earns its space twice: it is the machine members use when training alone, and the one a coach reaches for when a movement needs constraining.
features: Safe to work near failure without a spotter
Solo training, rehab progressions and accessory volume

coloured-bumper-plates-set-of-10-150kg.short: A coloured bumper plate set of 10, totalling 150kg — a complete platform loadout with colour-coded weights.
body: Ten coloured bumper plates totalling 150kg: enough to load a platform properly rather than approximately.
Colour coding is a working feature, not decoration. A coach calling a load from across the room, and a lifter checking a bar before pulling, both read colour faster than they read a printed number.
features: Bumper construction — designed to be dropped

coloured-bumper-plates-set-of-6-90kg.short: A coloured bumper plate set of 6, totalling 90kg — the starter platform loadout for a studio or home platform.
body: Six coloured bumper plates totalling 90kg — the smallest set that still makes a platform usable across a range of loads.
The right size for a single platform in a studio, a PT room or a serious home setup, where 150kg of plates would sit unused.

coloured-bumper-plates-set-of-8-100kg.short: A coloured bumper plate set of 8, totalling 100kg — a working platform loadout between the 90kg and 150kg sets.
body: Eight coloured bumper plates totalling 100kg: more increments than the six-plate set, less commitment than the ten.
The middle option, and usually the right one for a second platform on a floor that already has a full set on the first.
features: Bumper construction — designed to be dropped

coloured-bumper-plates-set-of-8-2-5kg-ch.short: A coloured bumper set of 8 with 2.5kg change plates, totalling 145kg — full loads plus the small jumps.
body: Eight coloured bumpers with 2.5kg change plates included, 145kg in total. The bumpers carry the load; the change plates make the small increases possible.
Without change plates a platform jumps in 5kg steps at minimum, which is too coarse for a lifter working near a limit. This set is the one that solves both problems at once.
features: Set of 8 plus 2.5kg change plates, 145kg total

competition-bumper-plates-set-of-10-150k.short: A competition bumper plate set of 10, totalling 150kg — calibrated plates for platforms held to competition standard.
body: Ten competition bumper plates, 150kg total. Competition plates are held to tighter weight tolerance and a consistent diameter, so a loaded bar sits at the correct height and weighs what it says.
For a floor that tests, competes or coaches to competition standard, that accuracy is the whole purchase.

competition-bumper-plates-set-of-8-100kg.short: Competition bumper plate sets of 8, in 100kg and 140kg totals — calibrated plates in two loadouts.
body: An eight-plate competition set, available in a 100kg and a 140kg total. Same competition tolerance and diameter, two levels of loading.
The 100kg suits a coached studio platform; the 140kg suits a floor whose lifters are working past it.

fixed-pu-curl-barbell.short: Fixed PU curl barbells from 5kg to 50kg in 2.5kg steps — a complete EZ-curl range with no plates to change.
body: Fixed curl barbells in polyurethane, running 5kg to 50kg in 2.5kg increments — nineteen bars covering the full range.

The case for fixed bars is throughput. On a busy floor, a member moving through curls, presses and rows picks up the next bar instead of stripping and reloading, and the station keeps moving. PU takes the handling that comes with that.
features: No plate changes — built for busy floors

lifting-plus-integrated-platform.short: The Lifting Plus integrated platform — a purpose-built lifting platform that protects the floor and defines the space.
body: An integrated lifting platform: the surface that takes dropped loads, protects the slab beneath it, and marks out where lifting happens.
A platform is as much a layout decision as an equipment one. It tells a room where the barbell work belongs, which keeps it away from walkways and machine traffic.
features: Protects the slab from dropped loads
Defines the lifting area within a floor

olympic-premium-rubber-weight-plates-3-g.short: Olympic premium rubber weight plates with 3-grip design, a set of 10 totalling 150kg.
body: Ten premium rubber Olympic plates totalling 150kg, with a three-grip design cast into the plate.
The grips are what make a plate manageable off a rack and onto a bar — a plate that can be carried properly is a plate less likely to be dropped on the way.

olympic-premium-rubber-weight-plates-3-g.short: Olympic premium rubber weight plates with 3-grip design, a set of 8 totalling 100kg.
body: Eight premium rubber Olympic plates, 100kg in total, with the same three-grip design as the larger set.
The smaller loadout, for a second station or a floor that does not need 150kg standing at every bar.

olympic-pu-weight-plates-4-grip.short: Olympic PU weight plates with 4-grip design, in 1.25kg, 2.5kg, 5kg, 10kg and 20kg.
body: Polyurethane Olympic plates with a four-grip design, available from 1.25kg through to 20kg — the full run, bought by the increment a floor actually needs.
PU is the hardest-wearing plate finish on a commercial floor: it holds its colour, resists chipping, and does not develop the smell rubber does in a warm room.

olympic-urethane-weight-plates-4-grip.short: Olympic urethane weight plates with 4-grip design, in 15kg and 25kg.
body: Urethane Olympic plates with a four-grip design in 15kg and 25kg — the two increments that fill the gaps in a standard plate run.
Urethane is specified where plates get handled hard and have to keep looking right doing it.

rubber-fixed-barbells-set-of-10-bars-rac.short: Ten rubber fixed barbells supplied with a rack — a complete fixed-bar station, bars and storage together.
body: Ten rubber fixed barbells and the rack to hold them, supplied as one station rather than as bars plus a storage problem.
Fixed bars keep a busy floor moving — no stripping, no reloading, no collars to find. The rack is what keeps them in weight order and off the floor.

rubber-fixed-barbells-set-of-5-bars-rack.short: Five rubber fixed barbells supplied with a rack — the compact fixed-bar station for studios and PT rooms.
body: Five rubber fixed barbells with their rack: the smaller station, for a studio, a PT room or a group fitness floor that needs a short range rather than a full one.
Same argument as the ten-bar set, at a size that fits a room where floor space is the constraint.
features: Compact station for studios and PT rooms

technique-training-pipe.short: A technique training pipe — a light bar for teaching lifting positions before load is added.
body: A light training pipe for coaching the Olympic lifts: it lets an athlete learn positions, timing and the path of the bar without any load to punish a bad rep.
Every coached weightlifting programme starts here. Cheap, and the piece of equipment that prevents the most injuries per dollar on the floor.
features: Teaching positions, timing and bar path

urethane-fixed-barbells.short: Urethane fixed barbells in 5kg, 7.5kg, 12.5kg, 17.5kg and 22.5kg — the half-increment bars for a fixed-bar range.
body: Urethane fixed barbells covering 5kg, 7.5kg, 12.5kg, 17.5kg and 22.5kg — the intermediate steps that fill out a fixed-bar rack.
Urethane is the finish for bars that are picked up and put down all day: it survives the rack and keeps its printed weight legible, which is what stops a member guessing.
features: Fills the half-increments in a fixed-bar range

3d-seated-abduction.short: A 3D seated abduction machine — glute and hip abductor work through multiple planes from a supported seated position.
body: Seated abduction with movement through more than one plane, so the glute medius and the hip abductors are loaded through the range they actually work in rather than a single fixed arc.
Supported seating keeps the trunk out of it, which is what makes this a machine a member can load properly without technique becoming the limit.
features: Glute medius and hip abductor work

4-stack-multi-station.short: A four-stack multi-station — four training positions on one frame, for compact floors and small facilities.
body: Four selectorised stations built into a single frame: four members training at once, on one footprint and one maintenance schedule.
The four-stack is the size that suits an apartment gym, a hotel facility or a small workplace floor — the widest programme available in the least space.

45-degree-hyperextension-bench.short: A 45-degree hyperextension bench — posterior chain work for the lower back, glutes and hamstrings.
body: A 45-degree hyperextension bench for back extensions, and for the glute and hamstring work the angle makes accessible.

Forty-five degrees rather than horizontal changes where the load sits through the movement, which is what makes this the version most commercial floors choose — and it is easier for a member to get into and out of unassisted.
features: Lower back, glute and hamstring work

5-stack-multi-station.short: A five-stack multi-station — five training positions on one frame, for facilities needing wider coverage in one unit.
body: Five selectorised stations on a single frame, for a floor that needs more of the body covered than a four-stack reaches without moving to individual machines.
The step most workplace and residential gyms take when one unit stops keeping up with demand at peak times.

8-stack-multi-station.short: An eight-stack multi-station — eight training positions on one frame, covering a full programme in a single unit.
body: Eight selectorised stations on one frame: effectively a whole gym's worth of programming in a single structure, with one install and one service visit.
For residential towers, hotels and corporate facilities, this is often the entire strength offering — which is why the number of stations matters more here than anywhere else.
features: Full-body programme in a single unit

abdominal-crunch.short: A selectorised abdominal crunch machine — loaded, progressive trunk flexion from a supported position.
body: Trunk flexion against a selectorised stack, so abdominal work can be loaded and progressed like any other lift instead of being left to unloaded repetitions.
The supported position also makes it accessible to members who cannot get up and down off a floor comfortably, which is a larger share of a commercial membership than most programmes assume.

adjustable-utility-bench.short: An adjustable utility bench — flat through incline to upright, the most-used bench on any free-weight floor.
body: An adjustable bench running from flat through incline to upright. Dumbbell presses, rows, shoulder work, supported curls — most of what happens on a free-weight floor happens on one of these.
Buy more than the plan calls for. The utility bench is the single most contended piece of equipment in a dumbbell area, and a floor is almost never short of machines before it is short of benches.
features: Adjusts flat through incline to upright
Dumbbell pressing, rows and supported work

alternate-leg-curl.short: An alternate leg curl machine — independent hamstring work, one leg at a time, correcting side-to-side imbalance.
body: A leg curl that works each leg independently rather than both together, so the stronger side cannot carry the weaker one through the set.
That is the entire argument for alternating machines: bilateral work hides an imbalance, unilateral work exposes and then corrects it. It matters most in rehab and return-to-play programming.

alternate-leg-extension-machine.short: An alternate leg extension machine — independent quadriceps work, one leg at a time.
body: Leg extension with each leg loaded independently, so a quadriceps imbalance shows up in the set instead of being masked by the stronger side.
Standard equipment in rehab-capable facilities, and increasingly in general commercial floors where members return from knee injuries and need to load one side at a time.

arm-curl.short: A selectorised arm curl machine — supported biceps work with the trunk taken out of the movement.
body: Biceps curls against a selectorised stack, with the upper arm supported so the movement stays at the elbow instead of turning into a swing.
Constraint is the point of a curl machine. It is also what makes it usable by members who have not yet learned to strict-curl a free weight.
features: Upper arm supported — isolates the elbow

belt-squat.short: A belt squat machine — heavy squat loading through the hips, with nothing on the spine.
body: A squat loaded through a belt at the hips rather than a bar across the back. The legs get the work; the spine is left out of it entirely.

That makes it the machine of choice for lifters training around a back injury, for high-volume leg work that would otherwise accumulate spinal fatigue, and for anyone who needs to squat without loading the trunk.
features: Load applied at the hips, not the spine
Heavy leg work with no axial loading
Training around back injury and high-volume work

biceps-curl.short: A selectorised biceps curl machine — isolated arm work on a fixed path, loaded from a stack.
body: A dedicated biceps curl station: fixed path, selectorised stack, and a pad that keeps the upper arm where it should be.
On a busy floor a curl machine takes pressure off the dumbbell rack, which is usually the most contested equipment in the room.
features: Takes load off the dumbbell rack

chest-press.short: A selectorised chest press — the foundation pressing machine for any commercial strength floor.
body: Seated chest press against a selectorised stack: the machine most members reach for first, and the one that gets a beginner pressing safely without a spotter or a bar.
There is no commercial floor that does not need one. It is the horizontal press for everyone who is not ready for, or not interested in, a bench and a barbell.

decline-chest-press.short: A selectorised decline chest press — pressing on a decline path for the lower chest.
body: A press on a declining path, which shifts the emphasis toward the lower portion of the chest and changes the shoulder position it works through.
The third press in a complete chest line, alongside flat and incline — the one that completes the angle coverage rather than repeating it.
features: Completes a flat / incline / decline press line

dual-adjustable-pulley.short: A dual adjustable pulley — two independently height-adjustable cable columns for the widest exercise range on the floor.
body: Two cable columns, each adjustable through its full height and each independently loaded. Between them they cover more exercises than any other single station on a gym floor.
Presses, pulls, rotations, chops, flyes, face pulls, rehab work — all from two pulleys and a set of attachments. It is the most programmable square metre in the room.
features: The widest exercise range of any single station

dual-arm-functional-trainer.short: A dual-arm functional trainer — independent cable arms for unilateral, rotational and sport-specific training.
body: Two independent cable arms, so each side can be loaded and moved separately — unilateral pressing and pulling, rotation, and the asymmetric patterns that sport actually happens in.
The independence is the feature. A fixed cable crossover ties the two sides together; a dual-arm trainer lets a coach programme each side on its own terms.

fixed-upright-bench.short: A fixed upright bench — a dedicated 90-degree bench for seated pressing and supported arm work.
body: A bench fixed at upright, with no adjustment to drift out of position. Seated shoulder pressing, supported curls, and anything that wants a vertical back support.
Fixed rather than adjustable means one less thing to break and one less thing to set wrong — worth having alongside adjustable benches on a floor that runs hard.
features: Seated pressing and supported arm work
No adjustment to fail or be set wrong

flat-bench.short: A flat bench — the plain, fixed bench a free-weight floor cannot have too many of.
body: A fixed flat bench. Bench pressing, dumbbell work, step-ups, a place to sit between sets.

Unglamorous and constantly in use. Flat benches are cheaper than adjustable ones and take the load off them, so a floor that buys enough flat benches finds its adjustable benches are actually available when a member wants an incline.

front-pulldown.short: A front pulldown machine — vertical pulling for the lats and upper back, loaded from a selectorised stack.
body: Vertical pulling to the front, against a selectorised stack. The foundation back machine on a commercial floor.

It is also the only way most members will ever train a vertical pull. A pull-up is out of reach for a large share of a general membership; a pulldown is the same pattern at a load they can actually work with.
features: Vertical pulling for lats and upper back

functional-trainer.short: A functional trainer — adjustable dual cables covering presses, pulls, rotations and rehab work in one station.
body: Adjustable cable pulleys in a single frame: pressing, pulling, rotating, and the full accessory and rehab vocabulary from one station.
For a floor buying one machine to serve the broadest possible programme, this is the answer. It is also the station PTs gravitate to, because it adapts to a client rather than the other way round.
features: Presses, pulls, rotations and rehab work
The most adaptable single station on a floor

glute-and-hamstring-developer.short: A glute and hamstring developer — GHD work for the posterior chain and loaded trunk extension.
body: A GHD: glute-ham raises, back extensions and loaded trunk work, with the hips fixed and the movement happening where it should.
The glute-ham raise is one of the few hamstring exercises that loads the muscle at both the hip and the knee, which is why it survives in strength and rehab programming long after fashions change.
features: Loads the hamstring at both hip and knee

hack-squat.short: A hack squat machine — supported squatting on a fixed path, with the back braced throughout.
body: Squatting on a guided path with the back supported against a pad, so the legs can be loaded heavily without the trunk becoming the limiting factor.
The machine members move to when they want quad volume that a barbell squat would not let them reach, and the one a coach uses when a squat pattern needs constraining.
features: Heavy quad loading without trunk fatigue

hi-and-low-adjustable-pulley.short: A high and low adjustable pulley — one cable column covering pulldowns, rows, curls and rotational work.
body: A single adjustable pulley column that runs from the floor to overhead: pulldowns and face pulls at the top, rows and curls at the bottom, rotations anywhere in between.
The economical way onto cable training when a dual station will not fit — one column, most of the exercise range.

high-row.short: A high row machine — rowing on a downward-angled path for the upper back and rear delts.
body: A row pulled from above the shoulder line, which changes the angle of attack onto the upper back and rear deltoids compared with a horizontal row.
Alongside a low row it gives a floor the two pulling angles a complete back programme needs.
features: Upper back and rear deltoid emphasis
Pairs with a low row for full angle coverage

hip-thrust.short: A hip thrust machine — loaded glute work without the barbell, pad and bench the free-weight version needs.
body: Hip thrusts on a purpose-built machine: the load is applied where it should be, the position is set, and there is no barbell to roll into place or pad to arrange.

The barbell hip thrust is one of the best glute exercises there is and one of the most awkward to set up on a busy floor. A machine removes every part of that friction, which is why these have become standard.

hip-thrustor.short: A hip thrustor — a dedicated loaded glute bridge station for hip extension strength.
body: A dedicated station for loaded hip extension: back supported, load carried at the hips, and a movement path that keeps the work in the glutes.
Hip extension is the most trainable strength quality in the posterior chain, and the one general members are most likely to have neglected.

incline-chest-press.short: A selectorised incline chest press — pressing on an incline path for the upper chest and front delts.
body: Pressing on an incline against a selectorised stack, working the upper chest and the front deltoids at an angle a flat press does not reach.
The second press in a complete chest line. A floor with only a flat press is under-serving half of its pressing programme.
features: Upper chest and front deltoid emphasis

iso-lateral-multi-squat-lunge.short: An iso-lateral multi-squat lunge machine — independent leg loading across squat and lunge patterns.
body: Squat and lunge patterns with each leg loaded independently, so the two sides can be trained and compared separately on the same machine.
Iso-lateral loading is what turns a leg machine into a rehab and athletic-development tool: the imbalance a bilateral squat hides becomes visible and trainable.
features: Squat and lunge patterns on one machine

iso-lateral-seated-row.short: An iso-lateral seated row — independent arm loading for rowing, correcting side-to-side pulling imbalance.
body: Seated rowing with each arm loaded independently, so a stronger side cannot take over the pull.
Rowing is where upper-body asymmetry shows up most clearly, and iso-lateral loading is the only way to train it out rather than around it.

iso-lateral-shoulder-press.short: An iso-lateral shoulder press — independent overhead pressing arms for balanced deltoid development.
body: Overhead pressing with independently loaded arms, so each shoulder works through its own range under its own load.
Particularly useful where one shoulder has restricted range or is returning from injury — the affected side can be loaded and progressed separately rather than held to the other side's pace.
features: Independent left and right pressing arms

lat-pulldown.short: A lat pulldown machine — the foundation vertical pull for lats and upper back, on a selectorised stack.
body: The lat pulldown: vertical pulling against a selectorised stack, with a thigh pad to anchor the lifter against the load.
One of the two or three machines that has to be on a commercial floor. It is how the majority of members train a vertical pull, and it scales from a beginner's first session upward.

lat-pulldown-and-seated-row.short: A combined lat pulldown and seated row — vertical and horizontal pulling in one machine and one footprint.
body: Both pulling patterns on one frame: pulldown at the top, seated row at the bottom. A complete back programme from a single footprint.
The combination machine is what a floor buys when it needs full pulling coverage and does not have the space for two separate stations.

lat-pulldown-circular.short: A circular lat pulldown — pulldown work on an arced path that follows the shoulder's natural travel.
body: A pulldown whose path arcs rather than running straight down, following the way the shoulder actually moves through the pull.
The arc changes where the resistance peaks through the range, which gives a floor a genuinely different pulldown stimulus rather than a second copy of the same one.
features: Different resistance curve to a standard pulldown

leg-extension-and-leg-curl-machine.short: A combined leg extension and leg curl machine — quadriceps and hamstring isolation in one footprint.
body: Both sides of the thigh on one machine: extension for the quadriceps, curl for the hamstrings, with the user changing position rather than the floor carrying two machines.
The sensible choice where floor space is the binding constraint and both movements are non-negotiable — which describes most small commercial gyms.
features: Leg extension and leg curl combined

leg-extension-machine.short: A leg extension machine — isolated quadriceps loading from a supported seated position.
body: Knee extension against a selectorised stack, with the hips and back supported so the quadriceps take the work on their own.
One of the few ways to load the quadriceps without also loading the hip and the spine, which is what makes it standard in both hypertrophy programming and knee rehabilitation.

leg-press-and-hack-squat.short: A combined leg press and hack squat — two heavy leg patterns on one frame and one footprint.
body: Leg press and hack squat combined: two of the heaviest-loading leg movements available, sharing a frame instead of occupying two.
Both are machines a serious floor wants and neither is small. Combining them is often the only way to have both in a room that also has to fit everything else.
features: Leg press and hack squat on one frame
Two heavy leg patterns, one footprint

linear-leg-press-45-degrees.short: A 45-degree linear leg press — heavy leg loading on a fixed path, with the back fully supported.
body: The classic 45-degree leg press: a linear path, a supported back, and the ability to load the legs far beyond what any squat variation allows.

The angle is what makes it work. A lifter can push genuinely heavy loads with no balance demand and no spinal loading, which is why it stays in programmes long after other leg machines are cycled out.
features: The heaviest leg loading on the floor

low-row.short: A low row machine — horizontal pulling from below for the mid-back, on a selectorised stack.
body: Rowing from a low anchor point, which puts the pull through the mid-back and the lats at an angle a high row does not reach.
The horizontal half of a complete pulling programme, and the counterweight to all the pressing a general membership does.

multi-belt-squat.short: A multi belt squat — belt-loaded squatting across several positions, with nothing on the spine.
body: Belt squatting with more than one working position available, so the same machine covers squats, split work and the variations a coach wants without loading the spine at all.
Belt loading is the reason to buy it: heavy leg work that can be programmed alongside a heavy pulling day without the two competing for the lower back.
features: Load at the hips, not the spine
Heavy leg work with no axial loading

multi-deadlift.short: A multi deadlift station — hip hinge and pulling patterns on a guided path, at a range of working heights.
body: A pulling station covering the hinge across several heights, so a lifter can work a full pull or a shortened range on the same frame.
A guided path is how a general membership gets the deadlift safely. It removes the two things that make a free-weight pull risky for an unsupervised member: bar path, and position under fatigue.
features: Guided hip hinge and pulling patterns

multi-hip-extension.short: A multi hip extension machine — glute and hamstring work across several hip positions.
body: Hip extension loaded across more than one position, so the glutes and hamstrings are worked through varied angles rather than a single fixed arc.
Standing hip work is the most transferable posterior chain training there is — it loads the hip the way walking, running and climbing stairs do.

multi-press.short: A multi press machine — several pressing angles from one station, covering chest and shoulder work.
body: A press that works at more than one angle, so flat, incline and overhead pressing come off a single station instead of three.
The efficient answer for a floor that needs pressing variety more than it needs pressing capacity — a studio, a workplace gym, or a second strength zone.
features: Multiple pressing angles from one station
Suits compact and secondary strength areas

olympic-decline-bench.short: An Olympic decline bench — barbell decline pressing with integrated uprights for an Olympic bar.
body: A decline bench with Olympic bar uprights built in: barbell decline pressing without improvising a rack and a bench together.
Completes a barbell pressing line alongside flat and incline. On a floor with a serious free-weight area, the decline is the one usually missing.
features: Completes a flat / incline / decline bench line

olympic-flat-bench.short: An Olympic flat bench — the barbell bench press station, with integrated uprights.
body: A flat bench with Olympic uprights: the bench press, which is the lift a free-weight floor is judged on.
Expect it to be occupied. A floor with one Olympic flat bench has a queue; a floor with two has a free-weight area that works at peak time.
features: The highest-demand station on a free-weight floor

olympic-half-rack.short: An Olympic half rack — squat, press and rack pull capability in roughly half a power rack's footprint.
body: A two-post half rack for squatting, pressing and rack pulls, with the working height and safeties of a full rack in far less floor.
For most commercial floors the half rack is the correct default. A full cage is only necessary where lifters routinely work to failure without a spotter.
features: Squat, press and rack pull work
Roughly half a power rack's footprint

olympic-incline-bench.short: An Olympic incline bench — barbell incline pressing with integrated uprights for an Olympic bar.
body: An incline bench with Olympic uprights built in, for barbell incline pressing at a fixed working angle.
The upper-chest counterpart to the flat bench, and the second barbell pressing station a free-weight floor should add.
features: Upper chest and front deltoid work

pec-fly-and-rear-delt.short: A combined pec fly and rear delt machine — chest and rear shoulder isolation from one station.
body: Both directions on one machine: pec flyes facing in, rear delt work facing out.

The pairing makes programming sense as well as spatial sense — the rear delt is the most commonly under-trained muscle on a commercial floor, and putting it on the same frame as the pec fly is the most reliable way to get members to do it.
features: Pec fly and rear delt on one station

pendulum-squat.short: A pendulum squat machine — squatting on an arced path that follows the body's natural squat mechanics.
body: A squat on an arc rather than a straight line, which tracks the way the hips and knees actually travel through a squat instead of forcing a linear path.

The arc changes the loading through the range and is markedly easier on the knees than a fixed linear machine, which is why pendulum squats have moved from specialist gyms onto general commercial floors.
features: Easier on the knees than a linear machine

power-grip-cable-attachment-set-5.short: A five-piece power grip cable attachment set — the handles that make a cable station worth having.
body: Five cable attachments, which is what turns one pulley into a dozen exercises: different grips, different angles, different muscles.
Attachments are the most commonly under-ordered item in a fit-out. A functional trainer with one handle is a fraction of the machine it was bought as.

preacher-bench.short: A preacher bench — strict biceps curling with the upper arm fixed against a pad.
body: The preacher bench fixes the upper arm against an angled pad, which removes the swing and the shoulder involvement from a curl and leaves the elbow to do the work.
Free-weight loading rather than a stack, so it takes barbells, EZ bars and dumbbells alike.
features: Angled pad fixes the upper arm
Takes barbells, EZ bars and dumbbells

pullover.short: A pullover machine — lat and serratus work through a movement free weights barely reach.
body: The pullover: an arcing pull through the shoulder that loads the lats and the serratus in a pattern almost nothing else on a gym floor covers.
It fell out of fashion and has come back, because the movement genuinely is not replaced by a row or a pulldown — the shoulder angle is different and so is what it trains.
features: A pattern not covered by rows or pulldowns

reverse-hyper.short: A reverse hyper — posterior chain loading and spinal decompression in one movement.
body: A reverse hyperextension: the trunk is fixed and the legs swing, loading the glutes, hamstrings and spinal erectors through the back of the hip.

The machine has a reputation for doing two things at once — building the posterior chain, and decompressing the spine on the return. That combination is why it is standard in powerlifting gyms and increasingly in rehab-capable commercial floors.
features: Posterior chain strength and spinal decompression

seal-row-bench.short: A seal row bench — chest-supported rowing with the torso completely taken out of the lift.
body: A seal row bench holds the lifter face down and elevated, so the row happens with no leg drive, no hip swing and no lower back involvement at all.
It is the strictest row there is. Everything the lifter can cheat with is removed, which makes it the honest measure of what the back can actually pull.
features: No leg drive or hip swing possible

seated-calf-raise.short: A seated calf raise machine — soleus loading through a bent-knee calf movement.
body: Calf raises with the knee bent, which shifts the work from the gastrocnemius onto the soleus underneath it.
Bent-knee and straight-leg calf work train different muscles, and the seated version is the one most floors are missing. It matters more than its reputation suggests for running and jumping athletes.

seated-leg-curl.short: A seated leg curl machine — hamstring loading from a seated position, with the hip flexed throughout.
body: Leg curls performed seated rather than lying, so the hip stays flexed through the movement and the hamstring is loaded from a different starting length.

Seated and lying curls are not interchangeable. The seated version puts the hamstring under load in a lengthened position, which is where most hamstring injuries happen and where the protective adaptation is worth most.
features: Loads the hamstring at longer muscle length

seated-row.short: A seated row machine — horizontal pulling with the chest supported, on a selectorised stack.
body: Seated horizontal rowing against a selectorised stack, with a chest pad taking the lower back out of the movement.
The most-used back machine after the pulldown, and the safest way for a general membership to train a horizontal pull at volume.
features: Chest supported — no lower back loading

shoulder-press.short: A selectorised shoulder press — seated overhead pressing with the back supported.
body: Overhead pressing against a selectorised stack, seated, with the back supported so the press stays vertical and the trunk stays out of it.
Overhead pressing is the pattern most likely to go wrong with free weights. A machine gives a general membership the movement without the technique risk.

squat.short: A squat machine — guided squatting with support, for loading the legs without a barbell.
body: A guided squat station: the pattern, the depth and the loading, without a bar across the back or the balance demand that comes with it.
It is the bridge between a leg press and a free squat — more demanding than the press, more forgiving than the barbell.
features: Bridges leg press and free-weight squatting

standing-abductor.short: A standing abductor machine — hip abduction loaded in a standing, weight-bearing position.
body: Hip abduction performed standing, so the glute medius is loaded while the leg is bearing weight — which is the position it actually stabilises in.
Seated abduction trains the same muscle in a position it never works in. Standing is the version that transfers to walking, running and single-leg stability.
features: Glute medius and hip abductor loading
Transfers to gait and single-leg stability

standing-multi-flight.short: A standing multi flight machine — multi-angle standing cable work for chest, shoulders and arms.
body: A standing station working through several flight angles, covering chest flyes, shoulder work and the arm patterns that sit between them.
Standing rather than seated brings the trunk into the movement, which is either the point or the drawback depending on the programme — for athletic training it is usually the point.
features: Multiple flight angles from one station
Standing — trunk engaged through the movement

triceps-press.short: A selectorised triceps press — isolated triceps loading with the upper arm supported.
body: Triceps pressing against a selectorised stack, with the position fixed so the elbow does the work and the shoulder does not take over.
The pressing counterpart to the arm curl, and the other machine that takes pressure off a busy cable station.
features: Takes load off the cable station

universal-abdominal-crunch.short: A universal abdominal crunch machine — loaded trunk flexion suited to a broad range of users.
body: Loaded abdominal crunching on a machine built to accommodate a wide range of body sizes and mobility levels.
The universal fit is what makes it work on a general commercial floor, where the same machine has to serve a first-week member and a long-term one without adjustment becoming a barrier.
features: Accommodates a broad range of users

universal-pulldown.short: A universal pulldown machine — vertical pulling sized and adjusted for a broad range of users.
body: A pulldown station built to fit a wide range of body sizes, so the same machine serves a broad membership without fighting the adjustment.
The vertical pull is non-negotiable on any floor. A universal fit is what keeps it usable by everyone who walks in.
features: Accommodates a broad range of users

v-squat.short: A V squat machine — squatting on a V-shaped path that tracks the body's natural line.
body: A squat machine whose path follows a V, which matches the line the hips and knees travel rather than forcing them onto a straight rail.
The result is a heavy squat pattern that most lifters find easier on the knees and lower back than a linear hack squat, while still loading the quads hard.
features: Tracks natural hip and knee travel
Heavy quad loading, easier on the joints

vertical-knee-raise-and-dip.short: A combined vertical knee raise and dip station — bodyweight core and triceps work in one frame.
body: Two bodyweight stations on one frame: vertical knee raises for the trunk, parallel dips for the triceps and chest.
Bodyweight stations are the cheapest capacity a floor can add. They need no stack, almost no maintenance, and they absorb traffic at peak time when every loaded machine is taken.
features: Vertical knee raise and dip combined

standing-hip-thrust-plate-loaded.short: The plate-loaded standing hip thrust — loaded hip extension from an upright position, using the plates already on your floor.
body: Hip extension loaded from standing, which trains the glutes in an upright, weight-bearing position rather than lying back on a bench. No barbell to roll into place and no pad to arrange.

This is the plate-loaded version: it takes the Olympic plates already on the floor, so the load goes as high as the plate rack does and the machine costs less than its selectorised twin. The trade is the time spent changing plates between sets, which matters more in a class than in a strength session.
A selectorised version of the same movement is listed separately.

standing-hip-thrust-selectorised.short: The selectorised standing hip thrust — upright loaded hip extension with a weight stack and a pin.
body: The same standing hip extension, loaded from a selectorised stack instead of plates. A pin changes the weight, so a member moves between loads in seconds and nothing is left on the floor.

That is what makes it the right choice for a busy floor or a circuit: the changeover is instant, the load is legible to a beginner, and there are no loose plates around a station people queue for. It costs more than the plate-loaded version and its top end is whatever the stack holds.
A plate-loaded version of the same movement is listed separately.
features: Instant load changes, no loose plates
